body.statement:
Let \(e\in\mathcal E\) have \(\mathcal I_e=\{i,j\}\), and suppose that \(T_e\) has rank one.  Put \(c_e=T_e(\cdot,z)/v_e(z)\), which is independent of \(z\).  Every factorization of this cell in \(\mathcal C_A(T)\) belongs to exactly one of the following disjoint modes (with the coincident case assigned to mode \({\rm E}\)):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
({\rm L})&a_{ei}\equiv0,\quad b_j=c_e,\quad b_i\ne c_e;\\
({\rm R})&a_{ej}\equiv0,\quad b_i=c_e,\quad b_j\ne c_e;\\
({\rm E})&b_i=b_j=c_e,\quad a_{ei}(z)=s_e(z),\quad
             a_{ej}(z)=v_e(z)-s_e(z),\quad0\le s_e(z)\le v_e(z);\\
({\rm D})&b_i\ne b_j,\quad c_e=q_e b_i+(1-q_e)b_j,\quad
             a_{ei}(z)=q_ev_e(z),\quad a_{ej}(z)=(1-q_e)v_e(z),
             \quad0<q_e<1.
\end{array}
\]
Conversely, every parameter tuple in one of these modes is a valid rank-one cell factorization.  Mode \({\rm E}\) is the disjoint union of the \(3^{|\mathcal Z|}\) split-coordinate faces obtained by declaring, for each \(z\), exactly one of \(s_e(z)=0\), \(0<s_e(z)<v_e(z)\), and \(s_e(z)=v_e(z)\).
body.proof_tex:
Selected-table positivity gives \(T_e(w,z)>0\) and therefore
\[
v_e(z)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}T_e(w,z)>0
\qquad(z\in\mathcal Z).
\]
Because \(T_e\) is nonzero and has rank one, all of its columns are positive multiples of one positive probability vector.  Normalization by their positive sums consequently gives a single vector \(c_e\in\Delta_{\mathcal W}^{\circ}\) such that
\[
T_e(\cdot,z)=v_e(z)c_e
\qquad(z\in\mathcal Z).
\]
For a cell factorization define the well-typed number
\[
q_z=\frac{a_{ei}(z)}{v_e(z)}\in[0,1],
\]
where the interval assertion follows from nonnegativity and
\(a_{ei}(z)+a_{ej}(z)=v_e(z)\).  Dividing
\(T_e(\cdot,z)=b_i a_{ei}(z)+b_j a_{ej}(z)\) by \(v_e(z)>0\) yields
\[
c_e=q_zb_i+(1-q_z)b_j. \tag{1}
\]
If \(b_i=b_j\), equation (1) and normalization give
\(b_i=b_j=c_e\), while the only remaining restriction is
\(0\le a_{ei}(z)\le v_e(z)\).  This is exactly mode \({\rm E}\), with
\(s_e(z)=a_{ei}(z)\).

Suppose instead that \(b_i\ne b_j\).  Subtracting (1) at two coordinates
\(z,z'\) gives
\[
(q_z-q_{z'})(b_i-b_j)=0.
\]
Since the vector \(b_i-b_j\) is nonzero, \(q_z=q_{z'}\) for every pair;
write the common value as \(q_e\).  If \(q_e=0\), then
\(a_{ei}\equiv0\), \(a_{ej}=v_e\), and (1) gives \(b_j=c_e\).  The
assumed endpoint inequality also gives \(b_i\ne c_e\), so this is
\({\rm L}\).  The case \(q_e=1\) is symmetrically \({\rm R}\).  If
\(0<q_e<1\), equation (1) and the displayed coefficient identities give
\({\rm D}\).  The alternatives are mutually exclusive by the endpoint
equality and the three disjoint possibilities for \(q_e\).  Substitution
into the factorization equation proves the converse in every case.  Finally,
since \(v_e(z)>0\), the three stated alternatives for each coordinate of
\(s_e\) are disjoint and exhaustive; their Cartesian product has
\(3^{|\mathcal Z|}\) members.
